title: Assessment of aspirin response in patients undergoing neuroendovascular treatments: A comparison of five platelet function tests across two platforms
content:
by Tasuku Sakayori, Kenji Shoda, Ryosuke Nakanishi, Yoshihiko Ueno, Ayumu Kanbe, Aki Oka, Daisuke Mizutani, Miyu Kitagami, Keisuke Kitano, Ryosuke Kikuchi, Yukiko Enomoto

Aspirin is widely used for periprocedural antiplatelet therapy in neuroendovascular procedures; however, variability in patient response poses clinical challenges. This study aimed to assess five platelet function tests on two different platforms: light transmission aggregometry (LTA) using the CN-6000 device and the VerifyNow system, which were utilized to assess patients undergoing neuroendovascular procedures. A total of 124 patients who underwent elective neuroendovascular procedures and received perioperative aspirin-based antiplatelet therapy between September 2020 and December 2023 were retrospectively reviewed. Platelet function was assessed at three time points: before surgery, 1–3 days after surgery, and 1 month following the procedure. The assessments included maximum aggregation (MA) induced by 1 mM arachidonic acid (AA), 10 μM ADP, and 1 μg/mL collagen, as well as collagen-induced platelet aggregation level (CPAL) and aspirin reaction units (ARU). Significant perioperative changes were observed only with 1 mM AA MA, which increased immediately after surgery (p < 0.001) and decreased at 1 month (p = 0.013), while other tests showed no significant differences. Correlation analysis revealed the strongest association between 1 mM AA MA and 1 μg/mL collagen MA (r = 0.65), followed by CPAL (r = 0.62). ARU correlated modestly with LTA-based measures (r ≤ 0.34). Receiver operating characteristic analysis identified CPAL >6.0 and collagen MA > 43.2% as equivalent to AA MA > 20%. In this cohort, perioperative changes were detected by 1 mM AA MA but not by the other platelet function tests, and correlations between VerifyNow ARU and LTA-based measurements were modest. However, the clinical significance of these differences remains to be established. Automated LTA using CN-6000 may offer a practical option for aspirin monitoring in patients undergoing neuroendovascular procedures. Further prospective studies are warranted to validate its clinical utility.
